analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell Medicare and Medicaid patients drugs at prices matching eight peer countries' lowest.
analysis.headline: One House Republican introduced a bill to force drug makers to charge Medicare and Medicaid patients the price rival countries pay; it drew zero cosponsors and has sat untouched in two House committees since March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation to run a five-year "Most Favored Nations" pricing model starting in 2029. Under it, drug makers would have to make their drugs available, to Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, at the second-lowest price the drug sells for in eight peer countries (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Switzerland, and the UK), adjusted for each country's purchasing power. A manufacturer could escape the mandate by signing an agreement with the Health Secretary that includes the same price terms plus a commitment to expand manufacturing in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be people enrolled in Medicare Part D drug plans, Medicare Part B (drugs administered by doctors and hospitals), and Medicaid, who would have access to covered drugs at the benchmark foreign price rather than US prices. Because these programs cover tens of millions of older and lower-income Americans, lower net prices could also reduce taxpayer spending and, depending on how plans set cost-sharing, reduce patients' out-of-pocket costs. The bill does not touch prices for people with private insurance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each drug manufacturer without a voluntary agreement to provide "access to the most-favored-nation price" of every covered drug to Medicaid beneficiaries, Medicare Part D enrollees, and Medicare Part B patients, and to the pharmacies, mail-order services, hospitals, and physicians that serve them [S2].

Defines that price as the second-lowest net price the drug sells for in any of eight reference countries — Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Switzerland, and the UK — counting all rebates and discounts and adjusting for purchasing power, so companies cannot hide behind inflated foreign list prices [S2].
Makes manufacturers report the pricing data the Secretary needs to calculate the benchmark price, and runs the model through CMMI for five years beginning January 1, 2029 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, through lower net prices on sales into Medicaid, Medicare Part D, and Medicare Part B. A good-faith concern is that lower revenues in large public programs could mean less money for research on future drugs, though the bill's purchasing-power adjustment and second-lowest (rather than lowest) price rule soften that. Taxpayers would likely save, not pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains a large escape hatch: the Secretary may suspend the mandate for any manufacturer "likely" to sign a covered agreement, and those agreements only require the same price terms plus a commitment "to the satisfaction of the Secretary" to increase US manufacturing — an open-ended pledge that could let companies avoid the demonstration model's enforcement while offering little verifiable in return [S2].

It is a test, not a permanent law: the model runs for five years starting January 1, 2029, and applies only to Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, so the roughly half of Americans with private insurance get no direct benefit [S2].

International reference pricing can cut drug-company revenue in big markets; critics of the approach argue that over time this can reduce incentives to develop new medicines, a cost an honest supporter of price controls has to acknowledge (this is a general feature of reference-pricing systems, not a claim from the bill text).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying idea targets a real and well-documented gap: Americans pay far more than people in peer countries for the same drugs. But this bill's design blunts its own punch — the mandate only starts in 2029, covers only public programs, lasts five years, and can be switched off for any manufacturer that promises the Secretary it will build factories in the US. How much patients actually save also depends on details the bill leaves to the Secretary, since it grants price "access" without dictating how plans and pharmacies pass the savings into lower copays. It is a signal-flare bill more than a working price-control law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2026 and sent to two House committees, which have taken no action on it; no vote has happened and the Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Meuser (R-PA) introduced the Most Favored Patient Act of 2026 on March 5, 2026, as the sole sponsor [S1][S2].
The same day, the House referred it to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — leaving it to each to consider the parts in its jurisdiction [S4].
No other member has signed on: the bill lists zero cosponsors [S3].
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off so far, because no price mandate has moved and none appears likely to before this Congress ends; Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries have gained nothing yet.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored it and zero members of either party cosponsored it, and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape is unknowable — though most-favored-nation pricing has unusually split loyalties, backed by President Trump while long opposed by many Republicans as price-setting.

industries.note: They would have to sell every drug covered by Medicaid, Medicare Part D, or Medicare Part B at the second-lowest price from eight peer countries — unless they sign an agreement with the Secretary trading the same price terms for a US manufacturing pledge. Their interest in defeating or diluting the bill runs directly against patients' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Hospitals and physician practices that administer Part B drugs
industries.note: Doctors' offices and hospitals would buy physician-administered drugs at the lower benchmark price, shrinking the markup they currently earn under the buy-and-bill system, though patients' 20% coinsurance on those drugs could fall too.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and Medicare Part D insurers
industries.note: Dispensers would obtain covered drugs for beneficiaries at the benchmark price, lowering their acquisition costs; whether patients share in the savings depends on how plans and pharmacies price the drug at the counter.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance. A bill with a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a split referral to two committees almost never gets a markup or floor time; unless Meuser builds a cosponsor list or Republican leadership decides to attach the idea to larger health legislation, this bill will most likely sit untouched until the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
